Chapter 1: A City on Edge—Sarajevo Before the Shot
Picture Sarajevo in the early 1900s. It’s so much more than just a maze of old streets and buildings—every stone in this city feels like it has its own story, carrying the weight of centuries. You can almost sense the history pressing in from the hills and those winding alleys, where empires have come and gone, leaving their mark on the people who call this place home. Shopkeepers, students, priests, soldiers... everyone could feel it. The tension, just hanging there in the air. Living in Sarajevo meant constantly balancing old traditions with the strange, new rules handed down by rulers far away.
In those years leading up to 1914, Sarajevo was a true crossroads. Ottoman minarets stood side by side with Austro-Hungarian facades, and if you wandered through the bustling markets, you’d hear a jumble of different languages swirling together. But underneath all that noise and color, there was a quiet unease. The Austro-Hungarian Empire had taken over Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they were determined to show who was boss. Their officials strutted around in crisp uniforms, speaking with foreign manners, never really seeing the people they governed. A lot of locals felt invisible in their own city—like strangers in a place that should have felt like home.
Now, imagine being young in Sarajevo at that time. The world felt both tiny and impossibly big at the same time. In school, you’d hear stories about distant emperors and epic battles, but step outside, and what you’d find was poverty and frustration. Many families barely scraped by. The hope of something better always seemed just out of reach. People looked for comfort where they could—maybe in family, maybe in faith. But more and more, some just held onto a quiet sense of resentment.
Out of this restless atmosphere, small groups of students started meeting in secret. These were kids full of energy and big ideas—dreaming of freedom, justice, and change. They whispered about revolution, read books that weren’t supposed to exist, and grew angrier each day at how their country had been sliced up by outsiders. Among them was a boy from a tiny village, thin and serious. He was a listener more than a talker, but he’d seen his own family struggle, and he knew firsthand what it felt like to be treated as less than others. For him, all the tension in the city wasn’t just political. It was deeply personal.
Of course, most people in Sarajevo just tried to get on with their lives, doing their best to ignore all the anger and hope swirling around them. But if you looked closely, you could tell—this city was like a powder keg, just waiting for a spark. The empire’s grip was slipping, and the old ways didn’t feel safe anymore. In smoky coffeehouses and shadowy back alleys, people argued about what the future should look like. Some dreamed of independence. Others worried about what chaos might come. But everyone, deep down, sensed that something was about to happen—even if no one could say exactly what it would be.
As the summer of 1914 crept closer, that anxiety only grew. News began to spread: there was going to be a royal visitor. An archduke from Vienna, sent to show off the empire’s strength. For the authorities, this was their big moment—a chance to prove they were in control. But for so many locals, it just felt like another insult. A reminder of how powerless they really were. In those tense days before the visit, soldiers started patrolling the streets, and rumors flew everywhere. Some people crossed their fingers, hoping it would all pass peacefully. But others, quietly, started to make plans.
